name: Tagom
confidence_why: Aldawi 2025 (with Aldawi 2022), working first-hand on Tagom with tone-marked data, shows a high/low register-tone contrast that marks tense, and the only dissent is Stevenson's 1956-57 survey, repeated second-hand by Tucker & Bryan 1966, which called the group "predominantly stress-languages" while itself recording three tone levels and admitting stress "has not been fully investigated"; lexical tone is still unchecked and no source says where word stress falls, so the hedged tonal-or-pitch accent coding is the clear winner on a thin record.
catalog_citation: Aldawi, Maha A. 2025. A first approach to Tagom verbal inflection and clausal negation strategies. In Helene Fatima Idris, Jan Junglas & Gertrud Schneider-Blum (eds.), Nuba Mountain Language Studies: Contemporary Perspectives, 71-104. Cologne: USB Monographs (open access;https://monographs.ub.uni-koeln.de/usbk/catalog/download/38/61/363).
catalog_quote: Vowel alternation is common in the phonology of Tagom; it is observed with TAM verbal conjugation, e.g., wɔ́-frə́k ‘you (SG) went/got out’/wə̀-frə̀k ‘you (SG) go/get out’, with wɔ́/wə̀ being the prefix for 2SG attached to the TAM-marked root frə́k/frə̀k ‘get out’ and the tone being responsible for TAM marking, as will be discussed in detail later. ... Tagom exhibits two register tones, a high tone and a low tone, which have a major role in its grammar marking (compare, e.g., ŋʊ́-lə́m ‘you (PL) saw’ with ŋʊ̀-lə̀m ‘you (PL) see’). The existence of lexical tone still needs to be checked.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tagom (Tegali) is described as a two-tone register language (H/L) whose tones mark tense/aspect (present = low tones, past = high, perfect = high-low, p. 80); the author says nothing about word stress or its position. The only stress statements in the literature are Stevenson's (1956-57: 47, snippets only): the Tegali-Tagoi languages are 'predominantly stress-languages', stress 'plays a marked role in sound change and may have grammatical (probably also lexical) significance, e.g. RASHAD: ome keyak The men eat, ome keyǝk The men ate', and tone is doubted; no placement rule is given. Bashir 2025: 49 (same volume, on Tagoi) argues Stevenson noticed the pitch contrast and attributed it to stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Stevenson 1956-57: 46-47 (quoted by Bashir 2025: 43) notes lax/short vowel variants 'particularly in unstressed syllables where they are also often lost or represented by some kind of neutral vowel', and that the neutral vowel also occurs in stressed positions; Stevenson 1964 SNR 45: 86 (snippet) 'Stress is important, and the vowels in unstressed syllables tend to..'. Aldawi 2025: 79 quotes Stevenson 1956-57: 49 that 'stress and vowel change also play a part in tense-formation' but does not confirm it for Tagom.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (verb roots with pronominal prefixes; tone alternations on prefix and root); elicited words and sentences from two Khartoum-resident Tagom speakers, 2017-2023. Stevenson's contrast keyak/keyǝk is a word-level grammatical (present vs past) contrast.
new_statements.identity_note: The only first-hand modern descriptions are of Tagom (= Gom = Rashad), the Rashad Town-Hills dialect of Tegali (Glottolog rash1248); Aldawi's Figure 1 places Tagom under the Tegali cluster together with Tegali, Umale and Kajakja. Stevenson's 1956-57 stress remark covers the whole Tegali-Tagoi (Rashad) group and its example is from RASHAD, i.e. the same variety. Nothing first-hand exists for Nuclear Tegali (nucl1243) beyond Meinhof 1916-17, which could not be opened.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Aldawi 2025 statement (tone language; two register tones with grammatical function; lexical tone unchecked): Tucker & Bryan likewise report tone (three levels rather than two) with no tonal doublets found, and add a hedged statement that stress also seems important, without a placement rule. The chapter covers the whole Tegali-Tagoi group and names RASHAD (= Tagom) as one of the two members of the Tegali Dialect Cluster; the p. 291 example is not labelled for dialect in the fragment. Everything is second-hand from Stevenson 1956-57 (AuU 40-41: 46-51).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given. The group (Tegali Dialect Cluster = Tegali and Rashad, plus the Tagoi cluster) is said to show three tone levels without tonal minimal pairs, and stress 'would also seem to have some importance' but was not investigated. The only placement datum is the verb pair yi-ko'rok 'I steal' / yo-ko'rok 'I stole' (p. 291): the stress mark stands before the stem-final syllable in both forms, i.e. stress stays on the stem (not on the subject prefix) across the tense contrast, which is carried by the prefix vowel. Vowels have 'subsidiary values I E O U in unstressed syllables' (sec. 1a, pp. 289-290).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the fragment notes only that I and U 'are not confined to unstressed syllables' (sec. 1a)
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan ch. 18b treats the Tegali-Tagoi group as a unit; its Tegali Dialect Cluster is 'TEGALI and RASHAD', and Rashad is the Tagom of the catalog (Glottolog rash1248 under tega1236). The p. 291 stress example is not attributed to a particular dialect in the fragment obtained. Meinhof's '11. Tegele' describes Tegele proper (from an informant not born in Tegele; the name appears as Togole in his text) and his '12. Rashad' (pp. 131-133) describes the speech of Rīsāt/Rešāt as 'ein Dialekt des Tegele', i.e. Tagom itself.

new_statements.quote: Tonlehre. Ich habe zumeist nur Starktöne bezeichnet. Nur einige Male, wo mir die musikalischen Töne besonders auffielen, habe ich sie angegeben. Ich glaube, daß man die Untersuchung der musikalischen Töne nur mit jemand vornehmen kann, der im Volk geboren und aufgewachsen ist. Zur Formenlehre. [...] [pp. 131-132, 12. Rashad:] ... zwischen Rashad und Tegele nur wenig Unterschied. Man vergleiche auch Tumale VI, S. 182ff. Zur Aufstellung einer Lautlehre und Formenlehre ist das Material zu unbedeutend. Ich gebe nur die Zahlworte und einige Vokabeln.
new_statements.translation: Accent/tone. For the most part I have marked only stress accents (Starktöne). Only a few times, where the musical tones struck me particularly, have I indicated them. I believe that the investigation of the musical tones can only be undertaken with someone born and raised among the people. On to the morphology. [...] [12. Rashad:] ... between Rashad and Tegele there is only little difference. Compare also Tumale, vol. VI, p. 182ff. The material is too slight to set up a phonology and a morphology. I give only the numerals and some vocabulary.

Meinhof 1917 on Tegele (= Tegali, the language of which Rashad/Tagom is a dialect; his Rashad notes have no phonology at all, pp. 131-132) transcribes dynamic stress (Starkton) on words ad hoc, notes pitch only where it struck him, and defers the study of tone to work with a native speaker: he neither asserts nor denies a tone system and states no rule for where stress falls (token scan of pp. 110-133 finds no other prosodic vocabulary). Compatible with the tonal coding and with Tucker & Bryan's hedged 'stress of some importance'; adds only the historical observation that stress prominence was what a 1914 fieldwor…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule. Meinhof says he mostly marked stress accents on individual Tegele words and occasionally musical tone where salient; tone investigation deferred; nothing on which syllable carries stress; for Rashad (Tagom proper) he gives numerals and words only, saying the material is too slight for a phonology and that Rashad differs little from Tegele.
new_statements.exceptions: none; p. 115 'betont' is syntactic emphasis ('.. betont wird z. B. udeni wāndis iek Vögel kamen und fraßen'), p. 105 'Betonung' belongs to instalment 10 (Lumun), not Tegele.
new_statements.identity_note: Tagom = the Rashad (Tegele/Risat) variety of Tegali (Glottolog tega1236, dialect rash1248 'Rashad Town-Hills'); Aldawi 2025 describes Tagom proper; Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 18b treats the whole Tegali-Tagoi group (TEGALI cluster = Tegali + Rashad; TAGOI cluster = Tagoi, Tumale, Moreb) from Stevenson's survey, and its p. 291 stress example is not labelled for dialect; Meinhof 1916-17 instalment 11 'Tegele' (pp. 110-131) and 12 'Rashad' (pp. 131-133) are word lists/notes from Tagoi-speaking and other informants about Tegele and Risat (Rashad).

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree on how much of the prosody is tone and how much is stress, and on the number of tone levels. Tucker & Bryan 1966 (p. 290, following Stevenson 1956-57) report three tone levels but no tonal doublets and say stress 'would also seem to have some importance', while Stevenson's own wording as previously snippeted (AuU 41: 47, held by the project from our earlier reading, not in this works list) calls the group 'predominantly stress-languages' and doubts that tone plays any important role apart from stress; Aldawi 2022/2025, first-hand and specifically on Tagom, describes two register tones (H/L) with a major grammatical role and says nothing about stress. No source gives a rule for where word stress falls; the one datum (yi-ko'rok / yo-ko'rok, p. 291) only shows stress remaining on the verb stem across a tense contrast. Meinhof 1916-17 could not be read and contributes nothing either way. No contradiction with the catalog. The catalog codes Tagom 'tonal' from Aldawi 2025 (two register tones H/L with grammatical function; lexical tone unchecked; nothing on stress). Tucker & Bryan 1966 ch. 18b (snippet fragments only; no open copy exists) report for the Tegali-Tagoi group three tone levels without tonal doublets plus a hedged 'stress would also seem to have some importance' and one stem-stress example, with no placement rule: compatible, a refinement.
